items.text: Does calling an AI's errors 'hallucinations' quietly smuggle in the assumption that it has real experiences?
Doesn't the thought experiment of swapping brain parts for silicon ones show consciousness could survive being moved into a machine?
If a computer simulation can't actually be conscious, what does that do to the idea that we're all living inside a giant simulation?
Do the four arguments against machine consciousness need each other, or does each stand on its own?
After arguing that digital computation likely can't produce consciousness, why does the author still leave the door open to artificial consciousness?
Given how uncertain every theory of consciousness still is, how sure can we really be that computation isn't enough for it?
If life matters for consciousness, should lab-grown brain tissue worry us more than any chatbot does?
Even once we're convinced a machine isn't conscious, can we simply stop feeling that it is?
Given how often we've wrongly denied moral status to animals and other people, might we be making the same mistake with AI?
